title: Give your dashboard structure
goal: Introduce your dashboard and make room for server information.
steps: Add a non-empty h1 and a paragraph introducing your dashboard.
Add a section with id=server-info containing a heading (h2).

hints.title: 1. Give content meaning
hints.text: Write HTML inside the existing <body>. Most elements have an opening tag, content, and a closing tag. Here is a different page:
hints.code:
My recipe book

Recipes I want to try.
hints.task: Choose your own dashboard heading and introduction. Which tag describes each piece of text?

hints.title: 2. Group related information
hints.text: A section groups related content. Its h2 heading introduces that group; h1 names the whole page.
hints.task: Adapt this structure for server information. Use the section ID requested in your mission, not recipes.

hints.title: 3. Connect IDs to later work
hints.text: An id is a unique name for one element. CSS and JavaScript can use it to find that element.
hints.task: Keep IDs unique. Check that your section contains its heading, rather than placing the heading after the closing section tag.

checks: A server information section with a heading

title: Make it your own
goal: Turn your server section into a readable information card.
steps: In style.css, give the body a background color other than transparent or white.
Give #server-info at least 12px padding and a visible border with width of at least 1px.

hints.title: 1. Match a selector to an element
hints.text: Put CSS rules in style.css. A tag selector matches every element of that type; # followed by an ID matches one element.
hints.task: Which selector matches the whole page? Which matches your server information section? Choose your own background color.

hints.title: 2. Make space inside a card
hints.text: Padding adds space between content and its border. Margin adds space outside the element. Values with px are lengths in pixels.
hints.task: Adapt the selector and choose padding that meets the mission’s minimum on every side. The example’s 8px is deliberately too small.

hints.title: 3. Draw a visible border
hints.text: The border shorthand combines a width, a line style, and a color. A width alone does not make a border visible.
hints.task: Try your own border style and color. Run the preview and check that you can see the card edge.

title: Add your first interaction
goal: Use a button to change a message without reloading the page. Keep your CSS.
steps: Add a button with id=greet and a visible text element with id=message.
In script.js, make clicking #greet change the text of #message to a non-empty greeting.

hints.title: 1. Find an element from JavaScript
hints.text: Put JavaScript in script.js. querySelector uses CSS selector syntax. A # means an ID. The starter HTML loads this file with defer, so the page elements exist when it runs.
hints.task: Use your mission’s IDs. If the browser console shows null, check the spelling and whether the element exists in your HTML.

hints.title: 2. Listen for an action
hints.text: A click listener runs a function when someone clicks a button. Defining the listener does not perform the click.
hints.task: Find your greeting button and attach a listener. What should happen inside that function?

hints.title: 3. Change what the page says
hints.text: textContent reads or replaces an element’s text. This example updates a recipe count, not a greeting.
hints.task: Combine this idea with your click listener to update the message element. Compare the text before and after clicking.

checks: The greeting button changes the message

title: Switch the atmosphere
goal: Connect JavaScript state to CSS with a reversible theme switch.
steps: Make each click switch the body's computed background color. A second click must restore it.

hints.title: 1. Let a class choose a style
hints.text: A class describes a reusable state or style. A selector like .highlighted applies only while that class is present.
hints.task: Create a class for your alternate page theme. Give it a different background from your normal page style.

hints.title: 2. Toggle a state
hints.text: classList.toggle adds a class when it is absent and removes it when it is present. It is useful when the same action must work in both directions.
hints.task: Your mission changes the page body, not a recipe card. How could your theme button toggle a class on that element?

hints.title: 3. Check both directions
hints.text: The class name in JavaScript must match the class name in CSS. You can inspect the body element’s class attribute to see whether it changed.
hints.task: Click once, then click again. If the class changes but the color does not, check your CSS selector and whether another rule overrides it.

checks: The theme changes and switches back

title: Meet your server
goal: Replace invented server information with a real response.
steps: Read /api/info using the API reference link.
On page load, fetch /api/hostname/ and put its hostname into a visible element with id=hostname.

hints.title: 1. Explore a real response
hints.text: An API returns structured data. The API reference opens /api/info. In this example we request that description, not the hostname.
hints.task: Find the hostname endpoint in the reference. Notice that await is inside an async function and that the function is called at the end.

hints.title: 2. Read one field from JSON
hints.text: After response.json(), the result is a JavaScript object. Dot notation reads a named field. This example is invented recipe data, not an API response.
hints.code:
const recipe = { title: "Vegetable soup", portions: 4 };
console.log(recipe.title);
hints.task: Which field does the hostname response contain? Read that field rather than displaying the entire response object.

hints.title: 3. Connect data to the page
hints.text: You already know how to select an element and change its text. The value can come from an object instead of a fixed string.
hints.task: Adapt the idea to your hostname element and fetched data. Call your loading function when the page starts; do not wait for a click.

checks: The hostname comes from the API

title: Bring the dashboard to life
goal: Display current information and communicate what happens during requests.
steps: Display values in visible elements with ids username, hostname, addresses, cpu, memory, memory-limit, and uptime. Keep numeric metrics in their API units; labels may surround them. Display N/A for null metrics.
Add a button with id=refresh that reloads all four endpoints. Also refresh automatically every 5 seconds.

While requests are pending, show Loading in a visible element with id=status. Clear Loading after completion. On a failed HTTP response or network failure, show Error or Failed there; a later successful refresh must clear the error.

hints.title: 1. Build one request at a time
hints.text: Start with the working hostname request. A small helper can read JSON from different endpoints. Check response.ok: fetch does not throw automatically for an HTTP 500 response.
hints.task: Use the API reference to discover each response’s fields. Add one endpoint and display its result before adding the next.

hints.title: 2. Show what is happening
hints.text: Use try for work that may fail, catch to report a failure, and finally for cleanup. This separate example reads the API description; it is not a dashboard refresh function.
hints.task: Instead of console messages, show loading, success, and errors in your status element. A new attempt must clear an old error. Remember to call the function you write.

hints.title: 3. Reuse an action for a button and timer
hints.text: Define your refresh function once, then pass its name to a listener or timer. Passing a function schedules it; adding () calls it immediately.
hints.task: Adapt this pattern for your refresh function and the mission’s interval. Timer delays are milliseconds: 1000 milliseconds is one second. Create the timer once, not inside the refresh function.

hints.title: 4. Handle lists and missing measurements
hints.text: An array can be joined into readable text. null means unavailable; 0 is still a real measurement. Avoid using value || "N/A", because that also replaces zero.
hints.task: Which API field is an array? Which metrics can be null? Keep numeric values in the requested units and label them so the reader knows what they mean.

hints.title: 5. Avoid overlapping refreshes
hints.text: If a request is slow, another timer tick or click might arrive before it finishes. A flag can help you keep only one refresh in progress.
hints.task: Keep earlier readings on screen while loading. Use Check my work to try delayed requests, errors, recovery, and null values that may not appear during a normal preview.

checks: All four endpoints supply the displayed values
HTTP failures are visible and recover
Network failures are visible and recover
